title: Names, Not Addresses: why the network needs DNS
prompt: Teach why DNS exists and what problem it solves.

protagonist.role: Backend engineer at a startup whose checkout API just moved behind a load balancer
protagonist.mission: Get the web app reachable again after the server IP changed
protagonist.stakes: Black Friday: 2 million orders a day, and every minute of downtime is about $18,000 in lost sales

problem_chain.problem: The app must be reachable from anywhere
problem_chain.naive_attempt: Hard-code the server IP in the frontend and in every client config
problem_chain.breaking_point: The load balancer is replaced and its IP changes; every client breaks at once
problem_chain.physical_analogy: A street address written in ink
problem_chain.demo: hard-coded IP returns connection refused after the move
problem_chain.unintended_consequence: The location cannot be stable, so the name must be

problem_chain.problem: Clients need a stable pointer to a moving location
problem_chain.naive_attempt: Put the name in /etc/hosts on every machine
problem_chain.breaking_point: Updating thousands of hosts by hand takes days
problem_chain.physical_analogy: A phone book that can be reprinted, versus names carved in stone
problem_chain.demo: dig example.com shows the name resolving to the new IP
problem_chain.unintended_consequence: The name now points somewhere, but the answer is cached

problem_chain.problem: Every lookup hitting the authority would melt it
problem_chain.naive_attempt: Rely on the lookup being fresh every time
problem_chain.breaking_point: A 24h TTL keeps serving the dead IP for a day after the move
problem_chain.physical_analogy: A photocopied directory that goes stale
problem_chain.demo: dig shows TTL counting down; stale answer served
problem_chain.unintended_consequence: Names are now a shared, cacheable resource — and a target

problem_chain.problem: Whoever controls the answer controls where traffic goes
problem_chain.naive_attempt: Assume the resolver always tells the truth
problem_chain.breaking_point: A poisoned cache redirects the checkout to an attacker
problem_chain.physical_analogy: A phone book someone can quietly reprint
problem_chain.demo: spoofed A record points the domain at an attacker IP
problem_chain.unintended_consequence: Naming solved reachability and created a new place to attack

abstraction_reveal: Every naming system trades a stable name for a mutable location, and that trade creates a cache and a place to lie — which is why TLS sits on top of DNS, not inside it.
must_pass: The protagonist (backend engineer, 2M orders, $18k/min) is named in the opening, not left as 'the reader'.
The hard-coded IP is shown working first and its failure is mechanical (a specific error after the move), not 'it doesn't work'.
DNS is defined in flow, before any resolver mechanics, and expanded on first use as Domain Name System.
At least one retrieval self-check (quiz or recall) appears after the demonstration of its beat.
The closing section maps each concrete fix to its general form and ends on what the reader can now do.
must_not: A bare acronym with only a functional gloss and no parenthetical expansion
An 'Appendix · Vocabulary' or separate glossary section inside the lesson
A quiz placed before the beat has demonstrated the concept
A section titled after the mechanism ('DNS record types') instead of the problem it solves

title: Constant Time: why hash tables exist
prompt: Teach why hash tables exist and what they replace.

protagonist.role: Backend engineer maintaining a session service for a social app
protagonist.mission: Look up whether a session token is valid on every request
protagonist.stakes: 40,000 requests/second, and a linear scan per lookup adds 90ms to every page load

problem_chain.problem: A token must be checked against a set of live sessions
problem_chain.naive_attempt: Scan the list until the token matches
problem_chain.breaking_point: At 40k rps with 200k live sessions, average 100k comparisons per lookup
problem_chain.physical_analogy: Reading every name in a phone book to find one
problem_chain.unintended_consequence: The scan must become a jump

problem_chain.problem: Halve the search space each step
problem_chain.naive_attempt: Keep the set sorted and binary-search it
problem_chain.breaking_point: Sessions are added and expired constantly, so maintaining sorted order costs more than the lookup saves
problem_chain.physical_analogy: A card catalog you must re-sort after every new card
problem_chain.demo: insert cost dominates; p99 lookup spikes on resize
problem_chain.unintended_consequence: Order is the wrong tool; we need a direct computation

problem_chain.problem: Compute the slot directly instead of searching for it
problem_chain.naive_attempt: Map each token to a bucket with a hash and store it there
problem_chain.breaking_point: Two tokens can hash to the same bucket and collide
problem_chain.physical_analogy: Mail slots by postcode: fast to file, but a slot can hold several letters
problem_chain.demo: hash('tokenA') and hash('tokenB') land in bucket 7
problem_chain.unintended_consequence: Collisions mean the bucket may hold a chain that grows

problem_chain.problem: As the table fills, chains grow and lookups slow back toward linear
problem_chain.breaking_point: At 0.9 fullness, average chain length triples and p99 crosses the SLA
problem_chain.physical_analogy: A post room with too few slots
problem_chain.demo: p99 latency curve vs. load factor; resize at 0.75 restores flat lookups
problem_chain.unintended_consequence: Resizing itself is a stop-the-world cost that must be amortized

abstraction_reveal: A hash table buys O(1) lookup by giving up order and by paying for it in collisions and resizes — the exact trade a sorted array refuses to make.
must_pass: The linear scan is shown working first, with its cost in concrete numbers tied to the 40k rps stake.
The hash function is defined in flow before any bucket notation, with one plain sentence.
Collisions arrive as the breaking point of the hash beat, not as a footnote.
Retrieval practice appears at least once, after the beat's demonstration.
The lesson ends on the general trade-off, not on a list of API methods.
must_not: An opening that lists 'arrays, linked lists, hash tables' before any is needed
A complexity table in section one, before the reader has felt a cost
Retrieval practice that asks the reader to recall a fact not yet demonstrated

title: One at a Time: why locks exist
prompt: Teach why locks exist and what problem they solve.

protagonist.role: Engineer at a ticketing company running a shared seat inventory
protagonist.mission: Stop selling the same seat twice when two users buy at the same instant
protagonist.stakes: 50,000 tickets/minute at launch; a double-sold seat triggers a refund, an angry customer, and a support call

concept_inventory: Atomic operations as the lighter fix

problem_chain.problem: Two requests read the seat count, both see 1, both decrement
problem_chain.naive_attempt: Read the count, decrement, write it back
problem_chain.breaking_point: Both write 0 for what should have been a sale of one seat; the seat is sold twice
problem_chain.physical_analogy: Two clerks reading the last ticket at the same moment
problem_chain.demo: interleaved log shows both threads reading 1 and writing 0
problem_chain.unintended_consequence: The read-modify-write must become one indivisible step

problem_chain.problem: Only one thread may hold the counter at a time
problem_chain.breaking_point: Correct, but now every purchase queues behind one lock; throughput collapses
problem_chain.demo: double-sells stop, but p99 latency climbs as the lock queue grows
problem_chain.unintended_consequence: Holding two locks at once can deadlock

problem_chain.problem: Two threads each hold one lock and wait for the other
problem_chain.naive_attempt: Lock the seat row, then lock the customer row
problem_chain.breaking_point: A thread holding seat waits for customer while another holds customer and waits for seat; both stall forever
problem_chain.physical_analogy: Two people in a doorway each waiting for the other to move
problem_chain.demo: thread dump shows two threads blocked, each waiting on the other's lock
problem_chain.unintended_consequence: Global lock ordering fixes it, but only if every caller obeys

problem_chain.problem: The counter needs no lock at all, only an indivisible decrement
problem_chain.naive_attempt: Use a compare-and-swap on the counter
problem_chain.breaking_point: Atomics fix this counter but do not protect multi-step invariants across two rows
problem_chain.physical_analogy: A turnstile that counts one person per click
problem_chain.demo: atomic decrement keeps throughput flat with no double-sell
problem_chain.unintended_consequence: Choose the lightest tool per invariant — the lesson, generalized

abstraction_reveal: Every concurrency fix buys correctness with contention: locks serialize, atomics narrow the critical section, and deadlock is the price of holding more than one thing at once.
must_pass: The lost update is shown as an interleaved read-modify-write, with the double-sell as the mechanical failure.
The lock is defined in flow before acquire/release syntax appears.
Deadlock is the unintended consequence that closes the lock beat, not a separate 'types of locks' list.
At least one retrieval self-check appears after the beat's demonstration.
The final beat generalizes to choosing the lightest tool per invariant, then hands over agency.
must_not: A glossary or vocabulary appendix collecting the terms at the end
A callout-heavy page where every paragraph is a warning box
Retrieval practice placed before the concept has been demonstrated
